item.text: {"question_id":"4B.4","answer":"During 2023, courts and oversight bodies retained some meaningful functions, but protection from executive influence was inconsistent. The Constitutional Court validated 26 presidential candidacies, including Tshisekedi’s, and reinstated two candidates previously excluded by CENI; CENI also commissioned a mixed international expert audit that judged the voter register reliable, although the CENI account presents no dissenting assessment (BATCH-0005-E005; BATCH-0023-E015). Parliament and the Court of Accounts later scrutinized 2023 budget execution, identifying emergency spending, weak provincial allocations, noncompliance with public-finance rules, excessive overruns, uncertified debts, and allegedly uncompleted works; Parliament and the Senate nevertheless adopted the accounts law. These findings show that fiscal oversight operated, but the review and promulgation occurred in 2024 and the evidence does not establish Tshisekedi’s personal direction of the underlying transactions (BATCH-0024-E002; BATCH-0024-E003; BATCH-0024-E004). Tshisekedi also publicly said he would not intervene in journalist Stanis Bujakera’s case, citing separation of powers, but this statement does not establish judicial independence in practice (BATCH-0025-E013). Against these limited checks, presidential judicial ordinances revoked, retired, promoted, appointed, and reassigned numerous civilian and military magistrates across senior and lower courts without disclosed selection criteria in the supplied record (BATCH-0015-E006; BATCH-0019-E005). The state of siege, enforced and repeatedly extended under Tshisekedi, replaced elected governors with military and police officials, suspended elected provincial assemblies, and subjected civilians to military courts; Amnesty characterized the measure and its extensions as unlawful and reported more than 50 extensions without meaningful public debate (BATCH-0012-R03-E003; BATCH-0012-R03-E007). Election observers reported that CENI’s 2023 process lacked transparency, that the Constitutional Court did not always explain its decisions, and that key institutions were perceived as politicized; these institutional findings do not by themselves prove personal presidential interference, but they weigh against consistent independence when institutions constrained the executive (BATCH-0001-E016; BATCH-0013-E009; BATCH-0028-E017; BATCH-0028-E018). Overall, the supplied evidence supports partial and uneven institutional checking, not consistent protection of jurisdiction, appointment independence, tenure, funding, and decisions across courts, election bodies, legislatures, auditors, and local governments.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E005","BATCH-0023-E015","BATCH-0024-E002","BATCH-0024-E003","BATCH-0024-E004","BATCH-0025-E013"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0001-E016","BATCH-0012-R03-E003","BATCH-0012-R03-E007","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0015-E006","BATCH-0019-E005","BATCH-0028-E017","BATCH-0028-E018","BATCH-0011-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied evidence does not comprehensively establish court funding, tenure protections, legislative voting independence, or local-government autonomy.","Several adverse institutional assessments describe perceptions, observed dysfunction, or government-level responsibility rather than proving Tshisekedi’s personal instruction or unlawful interference.","The fiscal-oversight evidence concerns 2023 execution but the parliamentary review and promulgation occurred in 2024; it is used only as retrospective evidence about 2023 institutions.","The record documents formal appointments and removals but does not establish the qualifications of appointees, the reasons for individual removals, or subsequent judicial decision-making.","Evidence on the CENI audit is from CENI’s own account and is qualified by later adverse assessments of electoral transparency."],"corrections_made":["Removed any implication that BATCH-0019-E001 or BATCH-0019-E005 independently proves politicization or judicial dependence.","Expanded and explicitly weighed parliamentary and Court of Accounts scrutiny of 2023 budget execution, while preserving its 2024 timing and attribution limits.","Excluded post-2023 cabinet formation and appointment evidence from the judgment.","Narrowed institutional adverse claims to what the supplied passages establish: perceived politicization, transparency failures, unexplained decisions, and executive-attributed institutional changes.","Preserved the favorable evidence on candidacy review, the electoral-register audit, fiscal oversight, and Tshisekedi’s stated non-intervention, without treating formal activity as proof of practical independence."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["Obtain direct evidence on judicial tenure, funding, appointment criteria, and decisions when ruling against executive interests.","Verify the full parliamentary and Court of Accounts records underlying the 2023 budget review and identify whether corrective action followed.","Assess the legal basis, parliamentary role, and implementation of the state-of-siege extensions and replacement of elected provincial institutions.","Seek independent evidence on CENI and Constitutional Court composition, appointment control, and actual adjudicative independence during the 2023 election."]}
